title: What training do agents need to sell long-term care partnership policies?
description: Long-term care partnership producer training: the DRA 2005 rule, the NAIC 8 hour and 4 hour standard, and verified Texas and California requirements.
shortAnswer: Agents selling qualified state long-term care partnership policies must be trained under a requirement added to the Social Security Act by the Deficit Reduction Act of 2005. Most states implement it through Section 9 of the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) Long-Term Care Insurance Model Act: a one-time course of at least 8 hours, then at least 4 hours every 24 months. Insurers must verify the training before the agent sells.
keyTakeaways: The federal hook is 42 U.S.C. 1396p(b)(1)(C)(iii)(V), added by section 6021 of the Deficit Reduction Act of 2005 (enacted February 8, 2006): states must assure that anyone selling a partnership policy receives training and demonstrates an understanding of it.
NAIC Model #640 Section 9B sets the common standard: a one-time training course of no less than 8 hours and ongoing training of no less than 4 hours every 24 months.

The training must cover partnership programs and their relationship to Medicaid, available services, alternatives to private coverage, inflation protection and suitability, and may not be insurer or product specific (Section 9B(2) and 9B(3)).
Insurers must obtain verification of training before a producer sells their long-term care products and keep partnership training records that let the state assure its Medicaid agency (Section 9C).

States can go further: Texas requires an 8 hour partnership certification course plus 4 partnership hours every reporting period, and California requires 8 hours in each of an agent's first four years and 8 hours before every renewal.
jurisdiction: United States (federal Medicaid requirement implemented through state insurance regulation; NAIC Model #640, with Texas and California as verified examples)
regulator: State insurance departments, including the Texas Department of Insurance (TDI) and the California Department of Insurance, working with state Medicaid agencies under rules set by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) and model laws from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC)
appliesTo: Licensed producers (life, or accident and health) who sell, solicit or negotiate long-term care insurance
Producers selling policies certified under a qualified state long-term care insurance partnership
Insurers issuing long-term care and partnership policies, for verification and recordkeeping
Continuing education providers offering partnership certification courses

sections.heading: Why does a long-term care partnership policy carry its own training rule?

blocks.text: Partnership policies affect a buyer's later Medicaid eligibility, so Congress made producer training a condition of a state's partnership program. Under [42 U.S.C. 1396p(b)(1)(C)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/1396p), a qualified state long-term care insurance partnership lets a state disregard assets equal to the benefits a partnership policy has paid, which protects those assets in Medicaid eligibility and estate recovery.

The partnership definition lists conditions the policy and the state must meet. One of them, clause (iii)(V), is the training rule: the state Medicaid agency provides information and technical assistance to the state insurance department "on the insurance department's role of assuring that any individual who sells a long-term care insurance policy under the partnership receives training and demonstrates evidence of an understanding of such policies and how they relate to other public and private coverage of long-term care." The clause was added by section 6021 of the Deficit Reduction Act of 2005, Pub. L. 109-171, enacted February 8, 2006.

Other partnership conditions shape what training must explain. Clause (iii)(IV) ties inflation protection to the buyer's age at purchase: compound annual inflation protection for buyers under 61, some level of inflation protection for buyers aged 61 to 75, and optional protection from age 76. Paragraph (5) requires partnership policies to meet specified provisions of the NAIC long-term care model regulation and model act as adopted as of October 2000.

sections.heading: What does the NAIC model require: 8 hours and then 4 hours?

blocks.text: Yes. Section 9 of the [NAIC Long-Term Care Insurance Model Act (#640)](https://content.naic.org/sites/default/files/model-law-640.pdf) requires a one-time course of no less than 8 hours before a producer sells, solicits or negotiates long-term care insurance, and ongoing training of no less than 4 hours every 24 months, as at November 2026. It applies to all long-term care sales in an adopting state, not only partnership policies.

blocks.title: NAIC Model #640, Section 9B(1)
blocks.text: "The one-time training required by this Section shall be no less than eight (8) hours and the ongoing training required by this Section shall be no less than four (4) hours every 24 months."

Section 9A(1) requires the producer to hold a producer license for accident and health or sickness, or life, and to have completed the one-time course. Section 9A(2) gave producers already selling long-term care insurance one year from the state's effective date to complete it. Section 9A(4) lets states approve the training as continuing education, so the hours normally count toward the general producer requirement described on the page on [insurance producer continuing education requirements](/regulations/insurance-producer-continuing-education-requirements).

sections.heading: What topics must partnership training cover?

blocks.text: The training must explain long-term care insurance, long-term care services, and, where applicable, the state's partnership program. Model #640 Section 9B(2) lists the minimum topics.

items: State and federal regulations and requirements, and the relationship between partnership programs and other public and private coverage of long-term care services, including Medicaid.
Available long-term care services and providers.
Changes or improvements in long-term care services or providers.
Alternatives to the purchase of private long-term care insurance.
The effect of inflation on benefits and the importance of inflation protection.

blocks.text: Section 9B(3) excludes training that is insurer or company product specific, and any sales or marketing information, materials or training other than those required by state or federal law. Texas adds Medicaid eligibility criteria, including financial eligibility, to its certification course outline in [28 Texas Administrative Code section 19.1022(g)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/texas/28-Tex-Admin-Code-SS-19-1022).

sections.heading: What must insurers verify and record?

blocks.text: Insurers carry the verification burden. Model #640 Section 9C(1) requires an insurer to obtain verification that a producer has received the required training before the producer is permitted to sell, solicit or negotiate its long-term care products, to keep those records under the state's retention rules, and to make the verification available to the commissioner on request.

Section 9C(2) adds a partnership-specific record. Insurers must keep records of producer training on their partnership policies that allow the state insurance department to assure the state Medicaid agency that producers received the Section 9B(2)(a) content and demonstrated an understanding of partnership policies and their relationship to public and private coverage, including Medicaid. The model's drafting note quotes the CMS State Medicaid Director Letter of July 27, 2006 (SMDL #06-019) and suggests states verify insurer compliance as an audit step in market conduct examinations and through annual random checks.

Because the federal test is "demonstrates evidence of an understanding," attendance alone is weak evidence. An assessment mapped to each required topic gives the insurer something to show the department; the guide on [how to design competency assessments](/guides/how-to-design-competency-assessments) explains how to build one.

sections.heading: How do Texas and California apply the requirement?

blocks.text: Texas follows the model's 8 and 4 hour structure through a voluntary certification, while California applies a heavier recurring requirement to all long-term care sales. Both are verified examples; other states' adopted rules should be checked with their insurance department.

items: **Texas certification:** under 28 TAC section 19.1022, an individual may not act as an agent for a long-term care partnership policy without a current Life, Accident, and Health license and completion of a partnership certification course of at least 8 hours. Agents already selling long-term care when the rule took effect had until January 1, 2009. Proof of completion must be kept for 4 years.

**Texas ongoing hours:** [28 TAC section 19.1023](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/texas/28-Tex-Admin-Code-SS-19-1023) requires at least 4 hours of TDI-certified partnership continuing education in each reporting period after the one in which the certification course was taken. A nonresident is excused if compliant with a home state that qualifies as a partnership state. Licensees with longevity exemptions from general CE are not exempt from this requirement.

**California:** [Insurance Code section 10234.93(a)(4)](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=INS&sectionNum=10234.93) requires agents licensed after January 1, 1992 to complete 8 hours of long-term care training in each of the first four 12-month periods from original license issue, and 8 hours before each license renewal after that. The initial training must be done before soliciting. Section 10234.93(a)(7) requires insurers to keep auditable procedures for verifying compliance.

sections.heading: What does an audit-ready training record look like?

blocks.text: The obligations split between the producer, the insurer and the state, and each leaves a distinct record. The table maps them for an insurer preparing for a market conduct examination.

blocks.text: Model #640 Section 9D treats satisfaction of the training requirement in any state as satisfying it in the adopting state, which helps multistate producers, but state-specific rules such as Texas's nonresident conditions still need checking. Refresh intervals that differ by state are easier to manage with the approach in the guide on [setting mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry represents the federal understanding test, the NAIC topic list and each state's hour rule as linked obligations, with assessment points attached to each required topic. That gives insurers evidence of understanding, not just attendance, for the Section 9C(2) records a state uses to assure its Medicaid agency.

faqs.q: Does the 8 hour course have to be repeated?
faqs.a: Under the NAIC model, no. The 8 hour course is one-time and is followed by at least 4 hours every 24 months. Some states differ: California requires 8 hours in each of the first four license years and then 8 hours before every renewal, so the answer depends on the state where the producer sells.

faqs.q: Can insurer product training count toward the partnership requirement?
faqs.a: Not under the model. Section 9B(3) of NAIC Model #640 excludes training that is insurer or company product specific and any sales or marketing content not required by law. Insurers can still provide product training, but it sits alongside the generic requirement rather than satisfying it.

faqs.q: What happens if a producer sells a partnership policy without the training?
faqs.a: The insurer should not have accepted the sale, because Section 9C(1) requires verification before a producer may sell its long-term care products. Consequences are set by state law, typically through market conduct findings and producer discipline. The federal statute itself places the assurance duty on the state, not on the individual producer.

faqs.q: Do longevity exemptions from continuing education apply?
faqs.a: In Texas, no. 28 TAC section 19.1023(f) states that licensees who qualify for the general CE exemptions in section 19.1004, such as the 20 year continuous licensure exemption, are not exempt from the 4 hour partnership continuing education requirement.
